fixes.explanation: That's the number in the text: “…a debtor owing ten thousand talents was brought to him.” (Matthew 18:24). Say it slowly, friend, because it's a mountain of a number. I think that debt is meant to feel enormous. That's a long way from pocket change.

A payment plan would have been nice, but that's not what the master orders. The text says he orders the man sold, “…along with his wife and children and everything he owned.” (Matthew 18:25). Nothing in the story offers him a work schedule. I think this is a heavy part of the story.

He does not cancel it. When that servant went out, he grabbed his fellow servant, began to choke him and said, “Pay back what you owe me!” (Matthew 18:28). He had just been forgiven so much. I'd call that a rough turn in the story.

That's what happened to the first servant, not the fellow servant. The master ordered that servant sold, along with his wife and children and everything he owned (Matthew 18:25). The text says the forgiven servant “…went and had the man thrown into prison until he could pay his debt.” (Matthew 18:30). It's easy to mix up the two debts, since there are two servants and two begging scenes.

Neighbors don't show up anywhere in this story. These servants were “greatly distressed” and “…went and recounted all of this to their master.” (Matthew 18:31). They took it straight to him. A group chat would've been faster, but the text says they went to their master.
